text: God supplies according to His riches in glory, not according to the stock market.
explanation:
"My God shall supply all your need according to His riches in glory by Christ Jesus." Not out of His riches, as if He'd spare a portion, but according to them, on a scale with all He owns. And His wealth doesn't rise and fall with the economy.

Abraham went through a famine and came out "very rich in livestock, in silver, and in gold." Isaac sowed in a year of famine and reaped a hundredfold the same year. Joseph's God-given wisdom turned Egypt into the world's breadbasket during seven lean years. When channels of income seem to close one after another, remember: you're in the world, but your supply isn't of it.

text: "Good measure, pressed down, shaken together, and running over." That's how Jesus describes God's giving back to you.
explanation:
Picture a boy raking dry leaves into a big wicker basket. They spring up loosely, so he climbs in and stamps them down, then rakes in more, shakes the basket to settle them, and keeps going until the leaves spill over the sides.

That's the picture Jesus chose: "Give, and it will be given to you: good measure, pressed down, shaken together, and running over." He wasn't embarrassed to talk about the harvest that follows giving, and you don't need to be either. "He who sows bountifully will also reap bountifully." Generosity isn't loss. It's seed.

text: Under law, the rich young ruler walked away with his wealth. Under grace, Zacchaeus gave half of his to the poor.
explanation:
In Luke 18, a rich ruler asks, "What shall I do to inherit eternal life?" Jesus gives him the law, and he boasts that he's kept it all, yet he can't part with his money and walks away sorrowful. One chapter later, Jesus gives Zacchaeus no commandment at all. He simply invites Himself to dinner.

Overwhelmed by grace, Zacchaeus stands up and says, "Look, Lord, I give half of my goods to the poor; and if I have taken anything from anyone by false accusation, I restore fourfold." The law demanded and got nothing. Grace demanded nothing and got everything. Generosity flows from a heart that's been loved first.

text: "Though He was rich, yet for your sakes He became poor, that you through His poverty might become rich."
explanation:
Some say this is purely spiritual: Jesus became spiritually poor so we could be spiritually rich. But Jesus was never spiritually poor. And the whole passage, two chapters long, is about giving money to the struggling believers in Jerusalem.

At the cross, He was stripped of everything. Among the last things He saw were soldiers gambling for His only garment. He took the curse of poverty so that you could be supplied. He paid a debt He didn't owe because you owed a debt you couldn't pay. Whatever part of His finished work you want to receive, it's yours to receive.

text: In Nehemiah's day, the high priest emptied the tithe room for Tobiah, whose name means "God is good."
explanation:
Tobiah was an enemy of Israel who mocked the rebuilding of Jerusalem's walls. Yet while Nehemiah was away, the high priest cleared out the large temple storeroom (where the tithes, grain offerings, wine, oil and frankincense were kept) and gave it to Tobiah. The Levites and singers went unsupported and left for their fields. Nehemiah came back, threw Tobiah's furniture out, and restored the tithes.

The irony is in the name: Tobiah means "the Lord is good." God is good, gloriously so. But that truth must never become an excuse that pushes out the things He loves, like giving, the Word and His house. "Why is the house of God forsaken?" Under grace, you don't have to tithe; you get to.

text: Levi "paid tithes through Abraham… for he was still in the loins of his father." Your giving can bless generations after you.
explanation:
When Abraham gave a tenth to Melchizedek, Isaac hadn't been born, let alone Jacob or Jacob's son Levi. Yet Hebrews says Levi was counted as giving through Abraham, because he was already in his great-grandfather's loins. Abraham's act of honouring God reached forward three generations.

And notice why the tithe is given: "Consider how great this man was." It's not mainly about getting rich; it's about honouring how great our Melchizedek is. "Here mortal men receive tithes, but there He receives them, of whom it is witnessed that He lives." Your giving testifies that Jesus is alive, and the blessing can flow to your children's children.

text: Generous people are "storing up for themselves a good foundation for the time to come."
explanation:
Paul tells Timothy to charge the rich "not to trust in uncertain riches but in the living God, who gives us richly all things to enjoy. Let them do good… ready to give, willing to share, storing up for themselves a good foundation for the time to come."

You may be living off a past harvest, but are you sowing for a future one? "While the earth remains, seedtime and harvest… shall not cease." Last time anyone checked, the earth still remains. When lean times come, generous sowers find their harvest waiting to meet them.
